author: Aditya Bansal
text:
KPMG doesn't just want to see your code. They want to see how you analyze growth. 📈

I recently came across a SQL interview question from a KPMG interview that perfectly captures the heart of business analytics: New vs. Repeat Customers.

📌The Problem:
How do you track the number of people who are buying from you for the first time versus those who are returning customers, broken down by date?

🎯The Twist:
If a customer makes multiple purchases on the same day, they should only be counted once. No "double dipping" for the same-day repeat!

🧠My Approach:
To solve this like a Senior Analyst, you need to:
1️⃣ Find the First Order Date for every customer using a Window Function (MIN() OVER).
2️⃣ Compare that "First Date" to the current order_date.
3️⃣ If they match? They're a New Customer. 🆕
4️⃣ If the current date is later? They're a Repeat Customer. 🔁

📌 Why this matters:
Any developer can join tables. But a Data Professional knows how to handle edge cases—like filtering out same-day duplicates—to give the business a true picture of retention.

author: Kushboo Chauhan
text:
🚨 Azure Data Factory Interviews Are NOT About Activities 🚨
Most candidates prepare ADF like this:
“Copy Activity, Lookup, ForEach, Data Flow…”
That’s exactly why interviews don’t go well.
In real ADF interviews, questions sound like this 👇
❌ “What is ADF?”
 ✅ “How do you build a centralized, reusable pipeline framework for 100+ pipelines?”
❌ “How do you read files?”
 ✅ “How do you handle schema drift, reprocessing, and idempotent loads?”
❌ “How do you monitor pipelines?”
 ✅ “How do you design logging, alerts, lineage, and audit trails?”
❌ “How do you deploy ADF?”
 ✅ “How do multiple developers work safely using Git integration + CI/CD?”
💡 What interviewers actually evaluate:
Can you design metadata-driven pipelines?
Do you think about retry, failure handling, and reprocessing?
Can you balance performance vs cost?
Do you understand security, Key Vault, RBAC, and auditing?
📌 If you’re preparing for ADF / Data Engineer interviews:
Stop memorizing activities
Start explaining architecture + scenarios
Always talk about scale, failures, and observability

author: Mohammad Affan
text:
Null values in data are unavoidable — and if you’ve worked with PySpark long enough, you know they can silently cause incorrect aggregations, broken joins, or misleading insights.
Early in my data engineering journey, I underestimated how much impact a few nulls could have. Over time, working with large-scale datasets, I learned that handling null values properly is not just a cleanup step — it’s a core part of building reliable data pipelines.
In PySpark, there are multiple ways to deal with nulls, and the “right” approach really depends on the business context. Sometimes filling nulls with defaults makes sense. Other times, dropping rows is safer. In some cases, filtering and flagging nulls helps uncover upstream data quality issues. I often rely on functions like
 fillna, dropna, isNull, and conditional logic using when to handle these scenarios carefully.

I’ve put together a simple visual with common PySpark patterns I use when working with null values in DataFrames — nothing fancy, just practical examples that come up in day-to-day work.

author: Aditya Bansal
text:
Most Data Engineers can write SQL, but 80% fail this "Gaps & Islands" question at Deloitte. 🛑
Why? Because it’s not about syntax—it’s about mathematical logic. 🧠

📌 The Scenario:
You're given a list of event dates. Some are consecutive (a "streak"), and some have gaps. 

🎯Your task is simple:
Group the streaks and find the Start and End date for each.

❌The Trap:
Most candidates freeze when they realize a simple GROUP BY isn't enough. If the dates aren't exactly the same, how do you group them?

🧠The Secret: It’s called the Difference Method. 🛠️
By subtracting a row sequence from your dates, all consecutive dates "anchor" to the same constant value. It’s one of those elegant patterns that separates senior engineers from the rest.

💡I’ve seen this exact pattern show up in Big 4 interviews more than almost any other. If you can’t handle "islands" of data, you'll struggle with real-world time-series analysis.

author: Sushma K L
text:
Most people say “I know SQL.”

But Data Engineer interviews quickly expose the gap.

After interviewing and reviewing many DE profiles, these are the SQL mistakes I see again and again 👇

❌ Common SQL mistakes in Data Engineering interviews
1️⃣ Thinking in SELECTs, not in JOINs
 Data rarely lives in one table.
 If 3–5 tables are involved and you freeze — that’s a red flag.

2️⃣ Avoiding window functions
 ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD
 Used daily in analytics, deduplication, SCDs — and loved by interviewers.

3️⃣ Hard-coding logic
 Fixed dates, fixed values, fixed assumptions.
 Data Engineers are expected to write scalable, dynamic SQL.

4️⃣ Ignoring NULL behavior
 One unexpected NULL can silently break aggregates or joins.
 COALESCE isn’t optional — it’s survival.

5️⃣ Weak GROUP BY fundamentals
 People use aggregates but don’t understand why queries fail.
 This shows immediately in interviews.

6️⃣ No explanation of thought process
 Even correct SQL gets rejected if you can’t explain:
 → why this join
 → why this window
 → why this aggregation

🎯 Reality check
SQL for Data Engineers is not about syntax.
 It’s about:
 ✔ thinking in datasets
 ✔ understanding data relationships
 ✔ writing production-ready logic

Fix the thinking.
The offers follow.

author: Atharva Thakare
text:
SQL Interview Questions for Data Engineers (Beginner → Advanced) 🚀

If you’re preparing for Data Engineering interviews, SQL is not optional — it’s your primary problem-solving tool.

Interviewers don’t just test syntax.
They test how well you think in data pipelines, transformations, and validations.

Here’s a structured breakdown 👇

🔹 Beginner Level (Foundations you must get right)

These test whether you understand how data is filtered and joined.

• Difference between WHERE vs HAVING
• INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL joins
• DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
• PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE KEY
• Handling NULL values
• COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column)

👉 If you struggle here, advanced SQL won’t help.


🔹 Intermediate Level (Daily Data Engineering SQL)

This is where real transformation logic starts.

• What are window functions and why are they used?
• Difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
• How to find & remove duplicates
• CTEs vs Subqueries — when to use which
• CASE WHEN for business logic
• UNION vs UNION ALL

👉 Most ETL logic lives at this level.


🔹 Advanced Level (Data Engineering Core 🔥)

These questions separate query writers from data engineers.

• How do you implement SCD Type 1 & Type 2 in SQL?
• How do you design incremental loads?
• What is MERGE / UPSERT, and when do you use it?
• How do you compare source vs target data?
• How do you handle late-arriving data?
• Partitioning vs Indexing
• How do you analyze an execution plan?

👉 This is where interviewers decide your level.


🔹 Scenario-Based Questions (Most Important 💡)

These test real project experience.

• Source has 10M rows, target has 9.8M — how do you debug?
• How do you make pipelines idempotent?
• How do you safely reprocess data?
• What SQL checks do you add before production release?
• How do you ensure data quality after ETL?

👉 There is no single “correct” answer — only good reasoning.


🔹 Final Advice

❌ Don’t memorize queries
✅ Understand why the query exists in the pipeline

SQL for Data Engineers is about:

Data correctness

Performance

Business logic

Reproducibility


If you can explain your thinking, not just the syntax then you’ll clear interviews.

text:
Finding duplicates is a daily task in SQL.

But the way you find them depends entirely on what you plan to do next:

Do you just need a count?
Are you trying to delete the extras?
Do you need to compare the conflicting rows side-by-side?

Here are 3 powerful ways to find duplicates in SQL:

1️⃣ 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗣 𝗕𝗬 + 𝗛𝗔𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚 ⮕ The Counter

This is the quickest way to see which keys have problems and how bad the duplication is. It’s the "bird's-eye view."

2️⃣ 𝗥𝗢𝗪_𝗡𝗨𝗠𝗕𝗘𝗥() ⮕ The Cleaner

Perfect for deduplication. By ranking occurrences, you can easily isolate the "extra" rows (WHERE rn > 1).

3️⃣𝗦𝗘𝗟𝗙 𝗝𝗢𝗜𝗡 ⮕ The Comparator

Great for deeper analysis. It shows you the conflicting pairs side-by-side so you can investigate exactly why they matched.

author: Ankita Gulati
text:
𝗗𝗮𝘆 𝟰/𝟯𝟬 — 𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝗤𝘂𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗧𝘂𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗗𝗘𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗚𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝗗𝗘𝘀

👉 What People Think…
“If the query works, that’s enough.”
“Performance issues = server problem.”
“Indexes magically speed everything up.”
“SELECT * is harmless.”

👉 What Actually Happens…
SQL performance depends on how efficiently your query interacts with data:
filters → joins → indexes → scans → execution plans.

The difference between a good query and a great query is often 10x speed.

🔟 𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗘𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿 𝗠𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄

1️⃣ Use Indexes Smartly
Indexes shine on high-cardinality columns.
Don’t index everything — it slows writes.

2️⃣ Avoid SELECT *
Selecting only required columns reduces scan time + network I/O.

3️⃣ Use EXISTS instead of IN (for large subqueries)
EXISTS stops after the first match → usually faster.

4️⃣ Optimize JOINs using indexed keys
Joining on unindexed columns is one of the biggest performance killers.

5️⃣ Filter Early (WHERE before GROUP BY/HAVING)
Shrinking the dataset early = faster computation later.

6️⃣ Avoid functions on indexed columns
WHERE DATE(timestamp) blocks index usage completely.

7️⃣ Prefer UNION ALL instead of UNION
UNION = deduplication = expensive sorting.

8️⃣ Don’t do wildcard-leading searches
LIKE '%text' → full scan.
LIKE 'text%' → index friendly.

9️⃣ Partition large tables
Especially for time-series data; improves pruning dramatically.

🔟 Always check the query plan (EXPLAIN)
Most engineers don’t — but this shows WHERE the bottleneck really is.

author: Nupur Zavery
text:
❌ I failed a SQL interview once because I didn’t know the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(1), COUNT(column), and COUNT(DISTINCT).

I thought they were all the same, but they’re not! Here’s a quick heads-up if you’re learning SQL or prepping for interviews.

- COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) count all rows, including NULLs.
- COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column.
- COUNT(DISTINCT column) counts unique, non-NULL values, ignoring duplicates.

This small difference saved me from future mistakes and confusion. I use COUNT almost every day now — and you should too!

author: Gaurav Kurhekar
text:
Hi All,

One of the interview questions which is mostly asked in Data Engineering : 

 How to normalize/Flatten the nested json once you have got the data extracted from upstream application via API integration?
-> Suppose you have got the data extracted from the upstream application via REST API (GET HTTPS METHODS) and it is in json format. 

𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟭 : First parse the json to an actual json format using json()
 data = json_data.json()

Now you have nested json like : 
data = [{'name': 'Vidit', 'age': 27, 'address':{'city':'Bengaluru', 'locality':'Electronic_City'}}]

 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟮: Now we can load the data into a Pyspark DataFrame like : 

 from pyspark.sql import functions as f

 df = spark.createDataFrame(data)

 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟯: Use explode() to flatten/normalize the json data into 1-D arrays :

 df1 = df.select(f.explode('address').alias('Address'))

 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝟰: Now select the columns out of the address column :

 df1.select([f.col('Address.city').alias('City'), f.col('Address.locality').alias('Locality')]).display()

 This is one of the ways out to flatten/normalize the JSON data in a Pyspark DataFrame. 

 Hope this will help you out!!

Databricks asked these advanced SQL + Delta questions in a Data Engineering interview (2+ YOE)
CTC – 20.9 LPA (Difficulty = Advanced)

2.⁠ Get the first and last login time per user from a huge events table (must be performant at scale).
3.⁠ Find top-3 customers by spend in each region using window functions and tie-breakers.
4.⁠ Detect duplicates in a transactional Delta table and safely deduplicate using MERGE (idempotent delete).

7.⁠ Compute a 7-day moving average of product sales on Delta Lake using event-time windows.
8.⁠ Pivot daily sales into month-wise columns (wide transform) and keep it streaming-friendly.
9.⁠ Find customers who bought at least once every month in a calendar year (set-based approach).
10.⁠ Rank products by yearly sales, reset ranking each year (window partition by year).
11.⁠ Find employees earning more than their department average (correlated subquery or window).
12.⁠ Calculate median transaction amount without a built-in MEDIAN (approx_percentile / percentile_cont approach).
13.⁠ Get all users who placed their first order in the last 30 days (first_value / row_number over partition).

15.⁠ Identify customers whose first and last transaction occurred on the same day (lifecycle edge-case).
16.⁠ Calculate monthly percentage of returning users (cohort + month-over-month retention).

18.⁠ Detect schema drift across historical Delta snapshots and propose remediation steps.

author: Shubham G.
text:
🔥 Completed One More Data Engineering Interview This Week!

This Week I had another Data Engineering interview, and I’m sharing a couple of important questions I was asked. Posting here so it helps others preparing for Azure + PySpark + SQL roles.

✅ 1️⃣ SQL Question: Identify Employees Sitting on Multiple Floors

📌 Requirement:
If an employee sits on multiple floors → print ‘Multiple’, else print the exact floor number.

SELECT emp,
 CASE 
 WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT floor) > 1 THEN 'Multiple'
 ELSE MAX(floor)
 END AS floor
FROM emp_table
GROUP BY emp
ORDER BY emp;

✅ 2️⃣ PySpark Question: Find Student Who Scored Highest Marks in Class 10

📌 Check at class level, not subject level.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Step 1: Total marks per student per class
student_total = (df.groupBy("class_id", "student_id")
 .agg(F.sum("marks").alias("total_marks")))

# Step 2: Rank students within class
w = Window.partitionBy("class_id").orderBy(F.desc("total_marks"))

result = (student_total
 .withColumn("rank", F.dense_rank().over(w))
 .filter((F.col("class_id") == 10) & (F.col("rank") == 1)))

result.show()

💡 Good interview overall — covered SQL aggregation logic and PySpark window functions.

If you’re preparing for Azure Data Engineer or PySpark-heavy roles, these scenarios are very common.

Happy Learning! 🚀

text:
Deloitte Data Engineer Round 2: The Interview I’ll Never Forget 🚀🔥
Last Thursday, 9:02 AM.
 Round 2.
 The real technical round.
 The round where you either prove your experience… or you’re out.
The interviewer started with a smile and said:
 “Let’s go deeper. Round 1 was just the warm-up.”
At that moment, I knew this wasn’t going to be about definitions.
 It was going to be about judgment, architecture, debugging, and real-world chaos.
Here are the exact Round 2 questions Deloitte asked me — and how I approached them calmly when most people panic.
1️⃣ “Design an end-to-end data platform for a fintech system.”
I explained a Lakehouse setup with Kafka + ADF + Delta + Databricks + Unity Catalog.
 Real-time + batch in one clean flow.
2️⃣ “Write a SQL to remove duplicates and keep the latest row.”
Used ROW_NUMBER with timestamp ordering.
 Simple. Clear. Trusted.
3️⃣ “Pipeline is successful but data is wrong. What do you check first?”
I said: row count, logs, joins, schema drift, checkpoint issues.
 They nodded immediately.
4️⃣ “How will you build a data quality framework?”
I shared my metadata-driven rule engine with a quarantine zone.
 This answer lands strong.
5️⃣ “Spark job takes 40 mins. Bring it under 10.”
Broadcast joins, AQE, repartition strategy, caching, cluster tuning.
 This answer alone filled half the interview.
6️⃣ “Incremental load without last_modified_date?”
Hash-based change tracking.
 They loved this.
7️⃣ “How do you handle duplicate Kafka events in streaming?”
Dedup with eventId + watermark + idempotent MERGE.
8️⃣ “Explain a 2 AM real production issue you solved.”
Logs → isolate partition → quarantine → fix → reprocess → RCA.
 Nothing impresses more than real experience.
By the end of the round, the interviewer said:
 “You think like an engineer, not just a coder. That’s what we look for.”
That sentence stayed with me.
Here’s the truth:
 Companies like Deloitte don’t care how many definitions you memorized.
 They care about your:
 • clarity
 • debugging sense
 • ownership
 • and ability to work under pressure

author: Surbhi Goyal
text:
Quick SQL question for everyone…

We all use column aliases to make queries cleaner. But have you noticed this?

You can use an alias in ORDER BY, but you can’t use it in WHERE.

Example:

SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY annual_salary; -- works

But this fails:

SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
WHERE annual_salary > 500000; -- alias not allowed here

Why do you think SQL allows aliases in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?

Curious to hear everyone’s thoughts.

text:
💼 Round 1 — The SQL Interview That Taught Me Simplicity 🎯

I walked into a Data Engineer interview thinking it would be all about Spark, ETL, and Big Data.
But the interviewer smiled and said —

“Let’s start simple. Write a SQL query to find the 2nd highest salary.”
I smiled back. Easy, right?
 Then he added —
“Make sure it works when two people have the same salary.”
That one line changed everything.
I paused… thought for 10 seconds…
 and wrote this:

SELECT salary 
FROM (
 SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk 
 FROM Employee
) ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;
He smiled. Round 1 had just begun.
Then the questions started coming like rapid fire 🔥

🧩 Find employees who earn more than their manager (self-join)
 📈 Get running total of sales by date (window function)
 🔗 Show all customers — even those with no orders (LEFT JOIN)
 🏆 Find top 3 customers per month (RANK + partition)
And finally —
“How would you optimize a SQL query running on billions of rows?”

I spoke about:
 ⚙️ Indexing join/filter columns
 🗂️ Table partitioning
 🚫 Avoiding SELECT *
 📊 Using materialized views

He closed his laptop and said —
“Good. You think like an engineer, not just a query writer.”
That hit hard.

It wasn’t about syntax.
 It was about clarity of thought — writing SQL that tells a story.

💡 Lesson I learned:
 Don’t chase 500 SQL questions.
 Master 50 — deeply.
 Understand why and how each query exists.
Because interviews don’t test your typing speed —
 they test how you think in SQL.

author: Gunja Singh
text:
⚙️ Round 2 — When SQL Turned Into an ETL Challenge 💡
After Round 1, I was confident.
 But Round 2 wasn’t about syntax — it was about data design thinking.
The interviewer started with —
“We process millions of records daily. How would you handle incremental loads?”
That one question shifted the entire tone.
 I wasn’t just writing SQL anymore — I was designing a pipeline.
I said:
 👉 “I’d capture the last successful load timestamp in a metadata table.”
 👉 “Then extract only records greater than that timestamp.”

SELECT *
FROM Transactions
WHERE LastUpdated > (
 SELECT LastLoadTime FROM Metadata WHERE TableName = 'Transactions'
);
He nodded. Then came the next twist —
“Now merge this data efficiently into the target table.”
I wrote:

MERGE INTO Target t
USING Source s
ON t.ID = s.ID
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE 
 SET t.Amount = s.Amount, t.LastUpdated = s.LastUpdated
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN 
 INSERT (ID, Amount, LastUpdated)
 VALUES (s.ID, s.Amount, s.LastUpdated);
He smiled — “Good. What about performance tuning?”
I explained:
 ⚙️ Index on join key
 🗂️ Partition by load date
 🧩 Batch commits
 🚀 Use staging tables
He closed with —
“You’re not just writing SQL. You’re thinking like an engineer.”
That hit me.
SQL isn’t just a language.
 It’s the backbone of every ETL — the logic behind every pipeline.

author: Gunja Singh
text:
💼 Round 1 — The SQL Interview That Taught Me Simplicity 🎯
I walked into a Data Engineer interview thinking it would be all about Spark, ETL, and Big Data.
But the interviewer smiled and said —
“Let’s start simple. Write a SQL query to find the 2nd highest salary.”
I smiled back. Easy, right?
 Then he added —
“Make sure it works when two people have the same salary.”
That one line changed everything.
I paused… thought for 10 seconds…
 and wrote this:

SELECT salary 
FROM (
 SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk 
 FROM Employee
) ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;
He smiled. Round 1 had just begun.
Then the questions started coming like rapid fire 🔥
🧩 Find employees who earn more than their manager (self-join)
 📈 Get running total of sales by date (window function)
 🔗 Show all customers — even those with no orders (LEFT JOIN)
 🏆 Find top 3 customers per month (RANK + partition)
And finally —
“How would you optimize a SQL query running on billions of rows?”
I spoke about:
 ⚙️ Indexing join/filter columns
 🗂️ Table partitioning
 🚫 Avoiding SELECT *
 📊 Using materialized views
He closed his laptop and said —
“Good. You think like an engineer, not just a query writer.”
That hit hard.
It wasn’t about syntax.
 It was about clarity of thought — writing SQL that tells a story.
💡 Lesson I learned:
 Don’t chase 500 SQL questions.
 Master 50 — deeply.
 Understand why and how each query exists.
Because interviews don’t test your typing speed —
 they test how you think in SQL.

author: Abilasha Veeraraghavan
text:
Trigger warning: Death, healing 

Back in 2019, death entered my home without offering the grace of a single warning.

I was neck-deep in work at office when I got a sudden call.
I had lost my mom.
What’s worse is that I had just spoken to her half an hour earlier. She was her usual chirpy self.

I was 21, new to the corporate world, and absolutely lost.
But this post isn’t about grief.
It’s about empathy.

I had just been onboarded onto a mega project with tight deadlines.
But my manager didn’t care about that.
She cared about me.

She gave me a month off with no questions asked.
She even came home to pay her respects, hugged me tight for 15 minutes.
She told my team: “Do not disturb her at any cost.”
And they didn’t.
They covered for me, checked on me every day, and made sure I could just… breathe.

That month officially became my crash course in adulthood.
I learned how to make a cup of tea without staining the kitchen walls.
Figured out what groceries we actually needed.
Discovered that “atta” isn’t just flour. It comes in multiple variants (some of which are totally useless, by the way!)
Realized that milk packets do, in fact, expire.
I was learning to manage a home, run errands... and somehow, keep myself together.

But even through all that chaos, I could almost hear my mom laughing, nudging me to find the good in everything.

And so I did.
Every little disaster became a lesson. Every small win, a reason to smile.

That phase changed how I saw workplaces and people.
Today, whenever I lead a proposal, project, or a team, I try to be that person.
The one who covers for others.
The one who makes space for someone to just be human.

People often ask, “Why do you go above and beyond for others?”
Because someone once did that for me, while I tried to navigate the unknown.
And that made all the difference. :)

author: Sanjeev Kumar Sahoo
text:
“We reduced database load by 70% — without adding a single index.”

Most devs jump straight to “Add an index” when queries get slow.
But sometimes, it’s not the database that’s slow — it’s how you use it.

Here’s what we found (and fixed):


1. Repeated Reads from the Same Table

Our service was hitting the DB ~40 times per user session — for the same data.
✅ Solution: Added a 30-second in-memory cache (Caffeine/Redis).
→ 40 queries → 1 query.


2. Chatty API Pattern

Frontend was calling 5 different APIs that all queried the same table.
✅ Solution: Aggregated data at backend and returned a single payload.
→ 5 round trips → 1.


3. Poor Pagination

Frontend was fetching entire datasets just to show 10 rows.
✅ Solution: Applied LIMIT/OFFSET and lightweight projection (SELECT id, name).
→ Response size dropped from 2MB → 80KB.


The Result

🚀 70% less DB load
💰 Infra bill down by 40%
⚡ Average response time: 600ms → 150ms


Real takeaway

Most performance issues aren’t about “bad queries.”
They’re about bad data flow.
If you reduce calls, you reduce load — instantly.

Have you ever solved a scaling issue without touching indexes or queries?

author: Sarita Jha
text:
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) - The Great Counting Myth

If you've worked with SQL long enough, you've probably heard this one:
 
"Never use COUNT(*); it's inefficient."

Sounds logical, right? After all, that * looks like it's counting every single column. But here's the twist, it doesn't.

COUNT(*) simply counts rows, not columns.
It's the database equivalent of counting people in a room, no questions asked, no forms checked.

COUNT(column), on the other hand, is pickier.
It only counts rows where that column has a non-null value.
Think of it as counting how many people brought popcorn to movie night. No popcorn? You don't get counted.

And here's the interesting part - in most modern databases, COUNT(*) is actually faster than COUNT(column).
Why? Because it doesn't need to inspect any column values. It can rely on metadata or index-only scans to get the row count efficiently.

Use COUNT(*) when you want to count rows. It's clean, correct, and optimized.
Use COUNT(column) when NULLs matter and you only want non-empty values.

author: Lan Chu
text:
Why don't LLMs produce the same output when given the same input, and at tempertaure = 0. A recent paper by Thinking Machines Lab has revealed the real culprit and offered a solution.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝗺𝗺𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝗼𝗻
For a long time, people believe it is inherent to how GPUs work. The typical hypothesis is that "concurrency + different floating point error" (𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 (𝘢+𝘣)+𝘤 ≠ 𝘢+(𝘣+𝘤))— which are introduced in GPU parallel operations causes nondeterminism. See example/screenshot in comment 👇 

However, this explanation is incomplete. Despite the fact that a GPU runs calculations in parallel, it actually does so in a completely deterministic way (i.e. it consistently puts the brackets in the same location).

The researchers from Thinking Machine Lab noticed this when the LLM always gave reproducible output when it was running in an isolated machine. So when did it start going wrong? When multiple users were logged in and asking the AI. That was their first hint: inputs.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐂𝐮𝐥𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐭: 𝐋𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐨𝐟 𝐁𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞
Most AI runs on big servers which is optimized to handle concurrent requests from millions of users. Instead of feeding each user request to the AI one by one, they are often bundles together in batches so that multiple requests can be processed in parallel, speeding up the response time dramatically.

Because each batch looks differently, the way the GPU decides to parallelize the calculation differs. Simply speaking, it might choose to put the brackets differently in the (𝘢+𝘣)+𝘤 ≠ 𝘢+(𝘣+𝘤) example.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐩𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻?
The solution proposed by Thinking Machines is to change the infrastructure to ensure that each batch that is loaded into the AI is consistently shaped. They call this batch-invariant kernels— meaning rewriting the core GPU operations from scratch so that calculations produce identical results regardless of how many users are being processed together.

Unfortunately for us users, we can’t do much about it. Need to wait for e.g OpenAI, Anthropic, etc. to adopt these changes.

Link to the paper in the comments. 👇

author: Harsh Gupta
text:
The “Simple” SQL Question That Stumps Everyone 
In my PwC interview, they asked:
👉 “Find the 2nd highest salary from the Employee table.”

I smiled — “Easy!” I thought.
But then came the trap… they asked: “Can you show me another way?”
…and then another.

That’s when I realized: this single question can expose how deep your SQL knowledge really is.

Here are 5 ways to solve it 👇

🧩 Problem Setup

Table: Employee

ID | Name | Salary
-------------------
1 | A | 5000
2 | B | 7000
3 | C | 6000
4 | D | 7000
5 | E | 8000

We need the 2nd highest salary = 7000.


🔑 5 Solutions

1️⃣ Subquery with MAX

SELECT MAX(Salary) 
FROM Employee
WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employee);

2️⃣ ORDER BY + LIMIT (MySQL)

SELECT Salary 
FROM Employee
ORDER BY Salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

3️⃣ RANK() Window Function

SELECT Salary
FROM (
 SELECT Salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS rnk
 FROM Employee
) t
WHERE rnk = 2;

4️⃣ DENSE_RANK() for duplicates

SELECT Salary
FROM (
 SELECT Salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS drnk
 FROM Employee
) t
WHERE drnk = 2;

5️⃣ CTE with NOT IN

WITH cte AS (
 SELECT MAX(Salary) AS max_sal FROM Employee
)
SELECT MAX(Salary)
FROM Employee
WHERE Salary NOT IN (SELECT max_sal FROM cte);

💡 Why this matters:

Recruiters don’t just check if you know SQL.

They test if you can solve the same problem in multiple ways.

This shows adaptability — a skill every data role needs.

author: Tajender Singh Katal
text:
Startup interview Question: (Senior Data Engineer)

I recently had the opportunity to participate in an interview process for a company I was very interested in. As part of the test, I was tasked with building an end-to-end data pipeline and encountered an interesting challenge:

Problem: For each (subscription_id, month) pair, keep only the latest record, without any updated_at or created_at timestamps!

Solution: In Spark, DataFrames are unordered by default, so I used monotonically_increasing_id() to simulate row ordering and identify the “latest” row. I had learned about this function in a Udemy course a while back, and this project gave me the opportunity to actually implement it and see how it works in practice. 😊 

Key Takeaways:

1) Prefer real timestamps whenever possible.
2) monotonically_increasing_id() is a handy fallback but only guarantees order within partitions.
3) Including ingestion timestamps during ETL is the best practice to avoid such issues.
It was a great exercise in thinking creatively about data ordering and pipeline design! 😊

author: Sachin M
text:
SQL 15/50 ( KPMG SQL Interview Problem)
Problem statement: 
Find and remove duplicate rows from a table based on specific columns, keeping only one unique row per duplicate group.

Input table: 

Customers

| customer_id | name | email |
|-------------|-----------|-----------------------|
| 1 | John Doe | john.doe@email.com |
| 2 | Jane Smith| jane.smith@email.com |
| 3 | Mike Jones| mike.jones@email.com |
| 4 | John Doe | john.doe@email.com |

SQL query (using CTE and ROW_NUMBER to keep one row per duplicate group): 

WITH CTE AS (
 SELECT *,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY name, email ORDER BY customer_id) AS rn
 FROM Customers
)
DELETE FROM CTE WHERE rn > 1;

Output table after removal: 

| customer_id | name | email |
|-------------|-----------|-----------------------|
| 1 | John Doe | john.doe@email.com |
| 2 | Jane Smith| jane.smith@email.com |
| 3 | Mike Jones| mike.jones@email.com |

SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);

SELECT e2.name as Employee

𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗺𝗮𝗽 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱 – Your Go-To SQL Roadmap

If you’re serious about data, you can’t afford to guess SQL.
This mindmap?
It’s everything you need, from basic SELECT to advanced analytics.

What you’ll find (and what actually matters):

1. SQL Basics:
SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY.
(Master these — 90% of interviews start here.)

2. Filtering, Sorting, Aggregations:
Use WHERE, BETWEEN, LIKE, IN, AND/OR.
Get your sums and averages with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, GROUP BY.

3. Joins (the real deal):
INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER — learn when to use each.
Most analyst rounds test joins, not fancy theory.

4. Window Functions:
RANK(), ROW_NUMBER(), LAG(), LEAD().
(Separates the real analysts from the copy-paste crowd.)

5. Date Functions:
Work with dates: NOW(), DATE_TRUNC(), EXTRACT() — saves you in reporting tasks.

6. CTEs, Temp Tables, Subqueries:
Write cleaner, reusable queries.
(Huge for complex dashboards or business logic.)

7. Performance & Optimization:
Use indexes, skip SELECT *, limit joins.
EXPLAIN your queries. Make them run faster, not just “work.”

How to actually learn:

Practice writing basic SELECT + WHERE + JOIN queries
Use free public datasets (Kaggle, Google BigQuery, etc.)
Challenge yourself with window functions & date logic
Build a sample dashboard (PowerBI/Tableau) using real SQL
Keep this mindmap open whenever you get stuck

This is the shortcut I wish I had when I started.

author: Sachin M
text:
SQL 1 / 50 ( SQL is Everywhere )
Google SQL Interview Problem:
- Given a table `employee` with columns `id`, `name`, `company`, `salary`, write a query to find the *median salary* in the company.

Example table:
| id | name | company | salary |
|----|---------|---------|---------|
| 1 | Alice | Google | 90000 |
| 2 | Bob | Google | 95000 |
| 3 | Charlie | Google | 100000 |
| 4 | David | Google | 105000 |
| 5 | Eve | Google | 110000 |
| 6 | Frank | Google | 115000 |

Solution:-
WITH RankedSalaries AS (
 SELECT
 salary,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS row_num,
 COUNT(*) OVER () AS total_rows
 FROM employee
)
SELECT
 AVG(salary) AS median_salary
FROM
 RankedSalaries
WHERE
 row_num IN ((total_rows + 1) / 2, (total_rows + 2) / 2);

This query works for both odd and even numbers of employees and gives you the median salary directly.

author: Irshad Ahamed
text:
This is a good starting point if you're trying to make sense of AI agents.

There’s a lot of talk about agent frameworks right now, but at the core, most of them build on the same set of ideas.

This cheat sheet gives a simple overview of the key building blocks—from LLMs to orchestration to protocols. Useful whether you’re exploring agent tooling, building internal automations, or just trying to understand the space better.

🔍 What is an AI agent?

Think of an AI agent like a smart personal assistant:

It doesn't just answer questions (like a chatbot), but can plan your day, book meetings, send emails, and make decisions based on context—automatically.

🧠 Language Model (LM)

This is the brain of the assistant. It reads your message and decides what needs to be done. But on its own, it can't actually do things like booking a ride.

🛠️ Tools

These are like the apps your assistant uses—Google Calendar, Uber, Email, etc. The agent accesses these through APIs and functions to take action in the real world.

🎯 Orchestration Layer

This is the task manager—it decides the order of steps, how to reason through complex tasks, and when to use which tool. It’s the difference between a smart assistant and one that panics with multitasking.

🌐 Agentic Protocols

These are like standard rules or networks that let assistants work across platforms (like coordinating between Slack, GitHub, and Email), and maintain memory over time.

🧱 Building AI Agents

There’s no single way to build an agent:

Some use a single smart prompt

Others rely on low-code platforms

Some build custom, end-to-end systems


The cheat sheet maps out these trade-offs clearly.

#aiagents #cheatsheet

author: Yashika Vaish
text:
🚀 Job Hunt Strategies That Actually Worked For Me – Data Analytics Edition
After working across firms like JPMorgan and Wells Fargo and recently navigating the job market myself, I wanted to share some practical, no-fluff techniques that helped me build momentum in my job hunt — especially in the data analytics space.
Whether you’re a fresher or a 10+ year experienced professional like me, these steps can give you a headstart:

🔍 1. Get Hyper-Clear on Your Niche
Don’t just say “Data Analyst.” Are you great at SQL & data transformation? Alteryx or Python automation? Storytelling with Power BI? Be specific. That clarity reflects in your resume, pitch, and interviews.

🛠 2. Build a Portfolio
You don’t need fancy dashboards — a simple Google Drive folder or GitHub with context is enough.

🤝 3. Reach Out, But With Value
Instead of “Hey, I’m looking for a job,” I’d write things like:
“Hi [Name], I noticed you’re working in [Company’s] data team. I’ve led multiple end-to-end analytics automations using SQL. Would love to learn more about your team and share ideas.”
It sparked real conversations.

📃 4. Resume Tip
Each bullet point should scream outcome + tech + complexity.
“Built dynamic dashboard in power bi to automate expense summaries across 8 LEs and 27 reports, reducing manual effort by 90%” — way better than just “Created reports.”

🧠 5. Practice Smart, Not Hard for Interviews
Don’t try to learn everything. I focused on:
 • SQL query challenges from real-world projects.
 • Data scenario-based questions I faced in JPM, EY, and Wells Fargo

👀 6. Post on LinkedIn (Even If It Feels Weird)
Sharing 1–2 lines about what you’re learning, building, or exploring creates visibility. I was surprised how many leads came from just being consistent here.

💡 If you’re in the data/analytics/product space and want help refining your job strategy, feel free to drop a message or connect!
Let’s help each other grow 🌱

author: Roshan Bakhade
text:
SQL Cross Question (Interviewer Style)

Q: Can we use both WHERE and HAVING in the same SQL query? If yes, which one is executed first and why?


✅ Answer:
Yes, we can use both WHERE and HAVING clauses in the same SQL query — and they serve different purposes in the query lifecycle.

🔸 WHERE filters rows before any grouping happens.
🔸 HAVING filters groups after aggregation (like SUM(), COUNT()).

📌 Execution Order:

FROM
WHERE → filters raw rows
GROUP BY
HAVING → filters grouped/aggregated data
SELECT
ORDER BY


Real Example:

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 50000
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;


🔹 WHERE → removes low-salary employees
 🔹 HAVING → keeps only departments with more than 5 such employees

text:
5 most asked SQL Interview Questions for Data Engineer jobs.

𝟭. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗧𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲

SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);

𝟮 . 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗿𝘀

SELECT e2.name as Employee
FROM employee e1
INNER JOIN employee e2
ON e1.id = e2.managerID
WHERE e1.salary < e2.salary

𝟯. 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗻𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿

SELECT name as Customers
FROM Customers
WHERE id not in (
SELECT customerId
FROM Orders);

𝟰. 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘁𝗲 𝗱𝘂𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀

DELETE p1
FROM Person p1, Person p2
WHERE p1.Email = p2.Email AND
p1.Id > p2.Id

𝟱. 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝗼𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗵.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR_MONTH FROM order_date) = EXTRACT(YEAR_MONTH FROM CURDATE() - INTERVAL 1 MONTH);

author: Pooja Pawar, PhD
text:
SQL Interview Series – Day 13 #KPMG⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝐓𝐚𝘀𝗸:⁣⁣
Write a SQL query to find the most recent order date for every customer in the orders table.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
This is a commonly asked question in SQL interviews at companies like 𝐊𝐏𝐌𝐆, 𝐙𝐒 𝐀𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗰𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 and 𝐃𝐞𝐥𝗼𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲, particularly for roles involving business analysis, reporting, and customer analytics. It evaluates your ability to apply aggregation functions and group-level logic in customer-focused data.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝐇𝗼𝘄 𝐭𝗼 𝐟𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝐢𝘁:⁣⁣
To solve this, group the records by customer_id, and use the MAX(order_date) function to identify the most recent order for each customer. This approach works well when you only need to retrieve the latest order date per customer and not the entire order details.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
This pattern is frequently used in loyalty programs, CRM updates, churn prediction, and behavioral segmentation.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝐂𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱:⁣⁣

1. 𝐆𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗣 𝗕𝘆 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲:⁣⁣
The dataset is grouped by each customer so that the aggregation function calculates one result per customer, rather than over the entire table.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
2. 𝐌𝐀𝗫() 𝐀𝗴𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:⁣⁣
The MAX() function retrieves the most recent (maximum) order date within each group of customer records. It’s efficient and supported across all major SQL platforms.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
3. 𝐀𝗹𝗶𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀:⁣⁣
The result of the MAX(order_date) is aliased as last_order, making the result more readable and suitable for further processing or export.⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
4. 𝐒𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗲-𝗢𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗦𝗰𝗲𝗻𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗼𝘀:⁣⁣
This method is ideal when you’re only interested in knowing when a customer last placed an order, not what they ordered or how much they spent.⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
5. 𝐄𝘅𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗙𝘂𝗹𝗹 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗥𝗢𝗪_𝗡𝗨𝗠𝗕𝗘𝗥():⁣⁣
If the interview question evolves to retrieving the entire latest order row per customer (including order ID, amount, or product), you can use ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC in a CTE or subquery.⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
6. 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲:⁣⁣
This logic is essential for scenarios like triggering re-engagement campaigns, identifying dormant customers, or updating dashboards with recent transaction summaries.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘀𝗸𝗲𝗱:⁣⁣
Interviewers use this question to assess your understanding of grouping and aggregation functions. It’s also a gateway into more advanced topics such as window functions, filtering over partitions, and analytics-driven reporting. Candidates who provide both basic and extended answers (using ROW_NUMBER() when needed) demonstrate readiness for real-world data challenges.⁣⁣
⁣⁣

The past 2–3 years tested me in every possible way.
While the world was navigating through uncertainty, layoffs, and recession —
I was quietly fighting my own battle: recovering from a major surgery, and rebuilding myself physically, mentally, and emotionally.
There were days when friends and colleagues were getting promotions, flying abroad, and achieving milestones —
and I was just trying to stand again, one day at a time.

When I was at my lowest, 𝐓𝐂𝐒 𝐡𝗲𝗹𝗱 𝗺𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴.
✅ They gave me projects with full WFH flexibility.
✅ They gave me time to heal, grow, and rebuild myself without fear.
✅ They never made me feel like a burden, even when I was lying on my bed while others were hustling in offices.
In a time when 𝐣𝗼𝗯 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 felt like a myth, TCS gave me exactly that.
That kind of support? Rare.
And 𝐈’𝐥𝗹 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆𝘀 𝗯𝗲 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹.

Growth often means stepping beyond what's familiar and safe.

So, with a heart full of gratitude,
𝐈’𝐦 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 — 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜’𝘃𝗲 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝗧𝗖𝗦 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗲.
Thank you, TCS, for being my foundation during the most crucial phase of my life.
Here’s to embracing new challenges, dreaming bigger, and writing the next chapter with courage.

author: Roshan Bakhade
text:
SQL cross interview questions :



🔸 1. Can you use WHERE and HAVING in the same SQL query?

✅ Yes, you can!
WHERE filters rows before any grouping or aggregation happens.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation is done.

🧠 Cross Question:
What happens if you apply a condition in HAVING that could be placed in WHERE instead?

✅ Answer :
Placing a non-aggregated condition (like salary > 50000) in the HAVING clause instead of WHERE can lead to:

🔸 Performance degradation — because:
SQL will first group and aggregate all data (even irrelevant rows),
then apply the filter.

🔹 On the other hand, using WHERE allows the database to filter early, reducing the amount of data processed in grouping — making the query faster and more efficient.


📌 Example:
-- ❌ Inefficient
SELECT department, AVG(salary)
FROM employee
GROUP BY department
HAVING salary > 50000; -- Not an aggregated condition


-- ✅ Efficient
SELECT department, AVG(salary)
FROM employee
WHERE salary > 50000 -- Filtered early
GROUP BY department;

author: Narendra Kushwaha.
text:
10 Real SQL Interview Questions (With Sample Answers)
For anyone preparing for developer or data roles, these questions are asked again and again.

Let’s dive in 👇

1. How would you find the second highest salary in an Employee table (without using TOP or LIMIT)?

SELECT MAX(Salary) 
FROM Employees 
WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);
2. Write a query to get the running total of sales per customer.


SELECT CustomerID, OrderDate, SalesAmount, 
SUM(SalesAmount) OVER (PARTITION BY CustomerID ORDER BY OrderDate) AS RunningTotal 
FROM Orders;
3. How do you handle NULLs in aggregations?
Use COALESCE() to handle NULL values:

SELECT SUM(COALESCE(SalesAmount, 0)) FROM Orders;
4. Difference between RANK(), DENSE_RANK(), and ROW_NUMBER()?

ROW_NUMBER() – unique numbers even if duplicates

RANK() – assigns same rank to duplicates, skips next numbers

DENSE_RANK() – assigns same rank to duplicates, no gaps

5. How to delete duplicate rows based on Email column:

WITH CTE AS (
 SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY Email ORDER BY ID) AS rn 
 FROM Users
) 
DELETE FROM CTE WHERE rn > 1;
6. How would you optimize a slow SQL query?

Add proper indexes

Avoid SELECT *

Use EXPLAIN or query planner

Filter early with WHERE

Minimize subqueries and joins

7. Customers who purchased in January but not in February:

SELECT DISTINCT CustomerID 
FROM Orders 
WHERE MONTH(OrderDate) = 1 AND CustomerID NOT IN ( 
 SELECT CustomerID FROM Orders WHERE MONTH(OrderDate) = 2 
);
8. DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP

DELETE – Removes specific rows, transaction-safe

TRUNCATE – Removes all rows, faster, minimal logging

DROP – Deletes the table structure itself

9. What are SQL Window Functions?
They let you calculate values across rows related to the current row without collapsing results:

SELECT Region, Salesperson, 
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY Region ORDER BY Sales DESC) AS Rank 
FROM SalesData;
10. How to pivot data manually without using the PIVOT keyword:


SELECT 
CustomerID, 
SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Jan' THEN Amount ELSE 0 END) AS JanSales, 
SUM(CASE WHEN Month = 'Feb' THEN Amount ELSE 0 END) AS FebSales 
FROM Sales 
GROUP BY CustomerID;
📘

author: Deimante Runaite
text:
My interviewer's Face When I Confused WHERE and HAVING: 😬
(A SQL Horror Story in 3 Acts)"

Act 1: The Setup
Me: "I built a predictive model in 72 hours!"
Interviewer: "Cool. What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?"

Act 2: The Panic
My brain: "They're... both... filters?"
My mouth: "HAVING is for... GROUP BY stuff?"
Interviewer's eyebrow: 📈 (reaching hairline)

Act 3: The Recovery
What I should've said:
→ WHERE = Filter before the party (raw data)
→ HAVING = Bouncer after the party (aggregated data)

Golden Example:
SELECT department, AVG(salary) as avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date > '2020-01-01' -- FILTERS ROWS FIRST
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 100000 -- FILTERS GROUPS AFTER

The Lesson:
You can know every JOIN type...
But if you blank on this, you look like you've only read about SQL.

Guilty confession: Which SQL basic still trips you up?

author: Shirin Khosravi Jam
text:
I’m a Data Scientist & I had to teach myself FastAPI
7 most important things for everyone should know
(also helpful for your interview 👇)

Because deploying AI/ML = building robust APIs.

1️⃣ 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 “𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗔𝗣𝗜”
→ It’s actually built on Starlette (handles web requests & async event loops) + Pydantic (validates and parses your data).
✅ That means super fast I/O and strict type checking.
✅ Know async def vs def - your DB calls, external APIs, file reads should be async. 
✅ That’s where you get real performance.

2️⃣ 𝗗𝗼𝗰𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲.
→ FastAPI auto-generates interactive Swagger docs at /docs from your Python type hints.
✅ Your contracts stay always in sync.
✅ Frontend teams, PMs, and even new devs love this - they can test endpoints right in the browser.

3️⃣ 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝘂𝗰𝗲.
→ With Depends(get_db), every request gets a fresh DB session.
→ Same pattern for auth checks, reading config, or injecting cache clients.
✅ Keeps your endpoints skinny, testable, and decoupled.

4️⃣ 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝘆 𝗣𝘆𝗱𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰.
→ Just define a BaseModel. 
→ FastAPI auto-validates request payloads, auto-serializes your responses, and gives clear error traces.
✅ No more if 'name' not in payload. 
✅ Safer, cleaner, faster APIs.

5️⃣ 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁-𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 & 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗵.
→ FastAPI ships with OAuth2, JWT flows, API keys.
✅ Even updates your Swagger UI to show an “Authorize” button.
✅ Know how to use OAuth2PasswordBearer or a Depends(verify_user). 

6️⃣ 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹.
→ Want to log every request? Measure execution time? Enforce CORS across your app? Or even modify headers before they hit your route?
✅ With @app.middleware("http"), you can wrap every single request & response globally.

7️⃣ 𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 & 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸𝘀.
→ Setup resources at startup (like DB connections), clean them on shutdown.
→ Use BackgroundTasks to offload sending emails, logs, or heavy processing after returning a response.
✅ Keeps your app snappy - user doesn’t wait for slow work.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜/𝗠𝗟?
Because eventually your model or AI system will live behind an API.
You need to handle inputs, validate them, async call your vector DB, log errors, and return JSON - all reliably.

My favorite quotes about data visualization:

1. "Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away." (Antoine de Saint-Exupéry)

2. "Numbers have an important story to tell. They rely on you to give them a clear and convincing voice." (Stephen Few)

3. "Visualization gives you answers to questions you didn’t know you had." (Ben Schneiderman)

4. "The ability to simplify means to eliminate the unnecessary so that the necessary may speak." (Hans Hoffman)

5. "There is no such thing as information overload. There is only bad design." (Edward Tufte)

6. "Data is the new oil? No, data is the new soil." (David McCandless)

7. "Data visualization is the language of decision making. Good charts effectively convey information. Great charts enable, inform, and improve decision making." (Dante Vitagliano)

author: Rajat Garg
text:
Here is how my interview at Amazon for SDE went (36 LPA)👇

This was an on-campus Amazon interview, and every round eventually came down to the same core skills:

📍 Round 1: Online Coding Round
2 DSA coding problems + MCQs on DBMS, code output, etc.

📍 Round 2: 1:1 DSA Interview
2 coding problems focused on Binary Search and Greedy logic.

📍 Round 3: 1:1 DSA Interview
Problems around Maximum Subarray and Binary Search.

📍 Round 4: Managerial Round 
Started with a simple DSA question, followed by a deep discussion on one project and behavioral questions like “Why Amazon?” and “How do you learn?”

Out of all candidates, only 3 were selected, and I was fortunate to be one of them.

I eventually chose Microsoft over Amazon, but this interview made one thing very clear to me:

👉 Top product companies test the same fundamentals, again and again.
DSA, problem-solving depth, CS basics, projects, and communication, not random tricks.
